explanations.explanation: That's the answer, friend, and Amos doesn't dress it up. He says, "It will be darkness and not light." (Amos 5:18) These people were counting down to the Day of the LORD, and Amos tells them the countdown is headed somewhere they don't expect. Wishing hard for a day doesn't change what the day is.

I get why that one's tempting. If you're longing for a day, you figure there's a prize at the end of it. But Amos says, "Woe to you who long for the Day of the LORD!" and then answers his own question: "It will be darkness and not light." (Amos 5:18) No prize in that, baker.

That's what a lot of folks were hoping for, I bet. Longing for a day usually means you think it's coming to rescue you. Amos has other news. He says the Day of the LORD "will be darkness and not light." (Amos 5:18) So the answer is darkness, not rest.

I see why you'd say that. Getting away from a lion sounds like a win, and in most stories it is. But the picture keeps going: the man who flees from a lion meets a bear (Amos 5:19). The man isn't safe, so this one is False.

That's right, baker. Amos says the man "flees from a lion, only to encounter a bear." (Amos 5:19) He gets away from one danger and runs right into another. Nobody in this picture gets to relax, and I think that's the whole point of it.

explanations.answer: He is bitten by a snake
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Amos says the man "enters his house and rests his hand against the wall, only to be bitten by a snake." (Amos 5:19) His own house! The one place a person figures is safe. I've leaned on plenty of walls in my day, and I'm checking mine from now on.

Home sweet home, right? That's what you'd expect when a man walks into his own house. But Amos flips it. The man rests his hand on the wall "only to be bitten by a snake." (Amos 5:19) No peace and quiet in that picture.

Nice thought, but the house in this picture has no good news waiting. The man rests his hand against the wall, "only to be bitten by a snake." (Amos 5:19) Amos is describing a day that keeps going from bad to worse, so a snake is the answer.

Yes, and the LORD says it plainly: "I hate, I despise your feasts! I cannot stand the stench of your solemn assemblies." (Amos 5:21) Those are strong words about gatherings the people were holding. I think that's worth slowing down for. The LORD is speaking, and He doesn't hold back.
You'd think so, since feasts and assemblies sound like good religious stuff. But the LORD says, "I hate, I despise your feasts!" (Amos 5:21) He isn't pleased with them at all, baker.

That would be a nice invitation, but it's not what He says. The LORD says, "I hate, I despise your feasts! I cannot stand the stench of your solemn assemblies." (Amos 5:21) More of them is the opposite of what He's asking for.

That's the word. The LORD says, "But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream." (Amos 5:24) Picture a river that never dries up and never stops moving. That's what He asks for, right after turning down the songs and the offerings.
Wisdom is a good thing, and the Bible loves it. But it isn't the word here. The LORD says, "But let justice roll on like a river…" (Amos 5:24) The river He pictures is justice.

Peace sounds right with a river, I'll give you that. Calm water and all. But the LORD's word is different: "But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream." (Amos 5:24) It's justice, with righteousness right beside it.

Right on, friend. The LORD says, "You have taken along Sakkuth your king and Kaiwan your star god, the idols you made for yourselves." (Amos 5:26) Notice who made them: the people did. A thing you build with your own hands can't be your king.
Altars came up in the neighborhood, since offerings were on the LORD's mind. But that's not what He calls them. He says Sakkuth and Kaiwan are "the idols you made for yourselves." (Amos 5:26)

I can see how that one slipped in, with all the feasts and assemblies around. But the LORD doesn't call Sakkuth and Kaiwan temples. He calls them "the idols you made for yourselves." (Amos 5:26) Sakkuth is called their king and Kaiwan their star god.

explanations.answer: Send them into exile beyond Damascus
explanations.explanation: That's the answer. The LORD says, "Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Damascus." (Amos 5:27) Damascus was a city, and beyond it means far from home. It's a heavy word, and I think it's worth saying so. The one speaking is "the God of Hosts."

explanations.answer: Give them peace in their own land
explanations.explanation: I wish the passage ended there, baker, but it doesn't. After "Therefore," the LORD says, "I will send you into exile beyond Damascus." (Amos 5:27) Exile means leaving the land, so peace at home isn't what's coming. It's a heavy ending.

explanations.answer: Raise up a new king to lead them
explanations.explanation: A new king is a fair guess, since Israel had kings on its mind. But that's not in this verse. The LORD says, "Therefore I will send you into exile beyond Damascus." (Amos 5:27) Exile is the answer, and it's a heavy one.
